summary: Summarizes accepted best practice for running public DNS-based blocklists for email and for mail server administrators who use them. It gives useful background, but does not judge whether particular lists work, or the concept overall. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some groups keep public lists of bad mail senders, checkable through the internet's phone book. This is a guide for the people running those lists and the people using them.

subtitle: How to run and use DNS-based blocklists for email reputation

tldr.problem: Since the 1990s, organizations have used DNS-based lists (DNSBLs) to share information about IP addresses and domain names involved in spam or abuse, but there was no standardized guidance on how to operate these lists responsibly or use them effectively without causing harm.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC outlines best practices for DNSBL operators covering transparency, listing and removal policies, technical operations, and graceful shutdown, and provides guidance for mail administrators on evaluating and using DNSBLs correctly.
tldr.outcome: DNSBL operators and users have documented best practices that improve trust, reduce false positives, and prevent accidental disruption to legitimate email.

facts.label: Recommended rescan period
facts.value: No more than once every 24 hours

today: RFC 6471 remains an influential guide for DNSBL operators and email administrators. While DNSBLs continue to be widely used, the document acknowledges they are controversial tools. The RFC does not judge the utility of DNSBLs overall or endorse any particular list, but establishes consensus operational practices that improve transparency, reduce false positives, and encourage responsible use across the email filtering community.

sections.title: What are DNSBLs
sections.content:
A DNSBL (DNS-based Blocklist) is a reputation system that uses the DNS (Domain Name System) to distribute lists of IP addresses or domain names associated with spam, open relays, open proxies, compromised hosts, or other abusive behavior. Mail administrators query these lists to filter incoming email.

DNSBLs emerged in 1997 as spam became a significant problem. The first DNSBL focused on identifying spam sources at static IP addresses. As spammers adapted by using botnets and open relays, additional DNSBLs were created to track new attack vectors. Today, over 700 public DNSBLs exist, plus private lists used by organizations internally.

The same DNS-based listing technology has been extended beyond email to whitelists (DNSWL), domain-name-based lists (RHSBL), URL lists (URIBL), and informational lists that return geographic, ASN, or reputation data. However, this RFC focuses primarily on public DNSBLs for email.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNSBL is a shared list of known bad email senders that mail servers can check. It started in the 1990s when spam became a big problem, and now there are hundreds of these lists.

sections.title: Operating a Responsible DNSBL
sections.content:
DNSBL operators must provide clear, honest, and transparent operations. The RFC emphasizes that operators should choose whatever listing criteria they wish, but those criteria MUST be clearly documented and consistently applied.

Operators SHOULD publish listing and delisting criteria prominently on their website, maintain an audit trail (while protecting sensitive information like spam traps), and disclose the scope and aggressiveness of their listings. Some DNSBLs list entire IP ranges when a few addresses show abuse, or use scoring systems where partial abuse triggers listing. These practices are acceptable if disclosed.

Listings SHOULD be temporary and expire automatically unless the listing reason still exists. Most importantly, DNSBL operators MUST NOT charge fees for delisting from negative-reputation lists, as this resembles extortion. Commercial DNSBLs may charge users for access, but not for removal from the list.
sections.plainLanguage: If you run a blocklist, be honest about how it works and what it blocks. Let people get off the list easily. Don't charge them to remove their address—that looks like extortion.

sections.title: Managing Listings and Removals
sections.content:
Operators SHOULD provide a simple, non-public way for affected parties to request removal. At minimum, the DNSBL should have a dedicated web form and email address separate from the listing criteria page. The operator MUST NOT use the DNSBL itself to block removal requests, and MUST respond within 7 days (SHOULD respond within 2 days).

Some highly automated DNSBLs benefit from a "no questions asked" removal policy, where any listed party can immediately request delisting. This creates a swift correction mechanism for false positives and prevents small disputes from escalating. However, automated systems can re-detect and re-list abusive behavior quickly, mitigating gaming of the system.

Delisting criteria SHOULD mirror listing criteria. If a listed entity meets all published removal requirements, the operator SHOULD NOT impose additional obstacles. Similar criteria for both listing and delisting builds user confidence in the DNSBL.
sections.plainLanguage: Make it easy for people to ask for removal. Respond quickly. Don't charge them. The removal rules should match the listing rules.

sections.title: Technical Best Practices
sections.content:
DNSBLs SHOULD use a subdomain structure (e.g., dnsbl.example.com rather than example.com) so DNSBL queries do not interfere with domain administration. Each logical zone SHOULD have its own DNS namespace and name servers, enabling clean separation of function and graceful shutdown.

Operators SHOULD provision adequate name server capacity with redundancy and DDoS mitigation. DNSBLs SHOULD publish test entries (conventionally 127.0.0.2 for IP-based lists, or "test" for domain-based lists) to allow users to verify operational status. Periodic testing by DNSBL users is essential, as DNSBLs may cease operation without notice.

Shutdown MUST be handled gracefully: operators must warn users for at least a month before shutdown and use techniques like pointing to non-existent test-net name servers to cause delays rather than returning bogus data. This prevents mail servers configured with DNS timeout issues from blocking all email when the DNSBL fails. Notably, a DNSBL MUST NOT list 127.0.0.1 or the entire Internet during operation or shutdown.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the right structure so DNSBL queries don't break normal domain stuff. Have backup servers. Let people test if the list is working. If you shut down, warn people and shut down slowly so they notice.

sections.title: Using DNSBLs Properly
sections.content:
Mail administrators SHOULD evaluate DNSBLs carefully before adoption, checking whether the list has a clear policy, a functioning website, community reputation, and a mailing list for announcements. Users SHOULD understand the intended use of each list—some apply only to direct peer IP addresses, not to IPs in email headers or web links.

Critical responsibility rests with the mail administrator: they MUST understand each DNSBL's policies and accept responsibility for filtering decisions made based on DNSBL data. A DNSBL without users cannot block email; the user makes the filtering decision and bears the consequences.

Users MUST test their initial DNSBL configurations to ensure they work correctly and SHOULD periodically check that DNSBLs are functioning properly. Common misconfiguration errors include querying wrong DNS zones, failing to set up local mirroring correctly, misconfiguring caching, or misunderstanding a list's intended scope. DNSBL operators SHOULD help users identify and remedy such mistakes.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using a blocklist, check if it is honest, well-run, and used by others. Understand what it's for. You are responsible for what you block. Test it. Monitor it.
